"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
**ml-ensemble-extremes · Ensemble size for rare extremes in a machine-learned weather ensemble.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · PASS

**Question.** Does 10 to 1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain probability forecasts, or does shared model error cap the skill?

**What is known.** HENS Part 2: 7,424 SFNO members per day for 92 summer-2023 dates; showed huge ensembles sample 4-sigma tails and reduce outliers. Whether AIFS-ENS, whose members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, keeps gaining skill past 50 members or saturates from shared model error.

**Hypothesis.** More members keep helping: 1,000 members sample top-percentile tails far better than 50, so extreme-event scores keep improving [s_hens].

**If compute is the lever.** Skill on top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain keeps rising past 50 members: 1,000 members sharpen the tails and improve extreme-event scores.

**If not.** Skill flattens near 50 members: members are exchangeable draws of one trained distribution, so shared model error caps tail sharpness and extra members add nothing.

**Test.** Run 7,000 fifteen-day AIFS-ENS v1 forecasts (7 dates x 1,000 members) on eight A100 40 GB GPUs; subsample 10-1,000 members, score top-percentile wind/temperature/rain probabilities against ERA5 with fair CRPS and Brier scores, and test whether skill still rises past 50 members.

*Compute axis.* Ensemble members per forecast: 10–1,000 members, 6 levels. Closest prior: 7,424 [s_hens], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Reproduce the published 4-minute N320 member time and 38 GB memory; one control run must match ECMWF open data within ensemble spread [s_crps_paper]. Tolerance: timing within +/-25% of 4 min; 38 GB memory fits; control field within the ensemble's own member-to-member spread at each lead time (GPUs are non-deterministic, so exact reproduction is not expected).

**Would not show.** Applies to AIFS-ENS v1 medium-range extremes on 7 dates; not a multi-season reforecast, other models, subseasonal leads, or direct proof that shared error causes any saturation.

*Cost.* Plans $963.17 of the $1,000 budget over 74.3 machine-hours, leaving $36.83. Main guess: peak filesystem usage [g], measured after $19.90 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 15× higher. Full scale: A 30-date multi-season reforecast at 1,000 members, $3,980, 3.98× the budget.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"All 1,000 members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, so past some N extra compute only shrinks the Monte Carlo error of the same (possibly wrong) distribution; the skill asymptote is a property of the model, not of N, and the run largely measures estimator convergence.\",\"assumption\":\"Ensemble members must all come from a single trained model; the axis of variation is member count.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the axis from member count to member diversity: first split the observed skill-vs-N curve into its Monte-Carlo-convergence part (estimable by resampling, no new forecasts) and its irreducible shared-model part; only if the latter dominates, spend compute on members drawn from different training seeds or checkpoints, so extra compute buys a different distribution rather than more samples of the same one.\",\"question\":\"At what member count does the Monte Carlo share of top-1% fair-CRPS skill (the fitted gap S_infinity minus S(N)) fall below 10% of the score spread between two independently trained model seeds?\",\"measure\":\"Resample the already-archived HENS 7,424-member, 92-date dataset into 10-1,000-member subsamples, recompute fair CRPS/Brier vs ERA5, fit skill(N) = S_inf - a/sqrt(N), and report the fitted asymptote gap at N=50 with bootstrap confidence intervals. Roughly $5-25 of CPU re-scoring; no GPU forecasts needed.\",\"compute_after\":\"If the MC share at N~50-100 is negligible, cancel the 7,000-member run and instead fine-tune a second seed (a fraction of the planned GPU budget) to test whether a mixed 2-seed ensemble shifts the asymptote.\",\"exact\":\"Fit S_inf - a/N^0.5 to bootstrap subsamples of HENS scores; report S_inf - S(50), its 95% CI, and the N where this gap reaches 10% of the seed-to-seed score spread.\",\"expected\":\"The gap at N=50 is already small relative to plausible model-to-model spread, meaning saturation is a model property and more members buy nothing.\",\"fails_if\":\"The fitted curve still rises materially past N=200, i.e., the Monte Carlo share is large and the original 1,000-member plan genuinely tests new territory.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS Part 2's own outlier-reduction curves with 7,424 members over 92 dates [s_hens], re-read as a convergence measurement rather than a skill result.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"With N members the finest resolvable probability is about 1/N, so fixed top-percentile scores conflate two things: better tail resolution (mechanical, scales with N) and better tail truthfulness (capped by shared model error). The metric saturates or rises for reasons orthogonal to the root question.\",\"assumption\":\"The event definition (top percentile of climatology, scored by Brier/fair CRPS) must be held fixed while N varies.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the measured quantity to one whose rarity scales with the compute: the error of the ensemble-implied return level at fixed physical thresholds (e.g., the 1-in-100-day 10 m wind gust and 2 m temperature), estimated by fitting a tail distribution to the pooled ensemble. This lets the question 'what does more compute buy' be answered as: access to rarer, still-accurate events, versus nothing.\",\"question\":\"Does the RMSE of the ensemble-derived 1-in-100-day return level for 10 m wind against ERA5 keep falling from N=50 to N=1,000, even where top-1% Brier skill has flattened?\",\"measure\":\"Fit GPD/GEV tails to subsampled HENS members (N in {10,25,50,100,200,500,1000,2000,7424}) for the 92 summer-2023 dates and compute return-level RMSE vs ERA5 over land grid points. Pure post-processing of existing data, roughly $10-30 CPU.\",\"compute_after\":\"If return-level error keeps falling where probability scores saturate, redirect the planned AIFS spend toward fewer dates at N=1,000 scored on return levels; if both flatten, the saturation conclusion is established without any new forecasts.\",\"exact\":\"RMSE of the 100-day return level, ensemble-derived vs ERA5, averaged over land grid points, reported as a function of N on the resampled HENS archive.\",\"expected\":\"Brier/fair-CRPS at the top percentile flattens by N~100-200 while return-level error keeps decreasing, showing that what extra members buy is tail resolution, not probability skill.\",\"fails_if\":\"Return-level error also flattens by N~100, which would show the cap is real and shared even on the resolution-insensitive quantity.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS's claim of sampling 4-sigma tails [s_hens], recast as return-level accuracy rather than counts of sampled outliers.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The binding statistical constraint is independent weather cases, not members: members on the same date are correlated evidence about one event, so pushing N from 50 to 1,000 on only 7 dates may buy more of the same while the yes/no slope past N=50 stays undetectable regardless of member count.\",\"assumption\":\"The number of verification dates is fixed at 7 and ensemble size is the free compute axis; all members must be run before any scoring.\",\"reframe\":\"Swap the compute axis and reorder the work: before running anything, test whether 7 dates can resolve a slope at all; if not, reallocate the same budget from 1,000 members x 7 dates to ~100-200 members x 40-60 dates, and run members in sequential batches with a stopping rule once the slope's sign is resolved.\",\"question\":\"With 7 dates, what is the smallest skill-vs-log(N) slope past N=50 in fair CRPS for top-1% events that is detectable at 80% power?\",\"measure\":\"Bootstrap power analysis on the existing 92-date HENS archive: repeatedly subsample 7 dates, compute the OLS slope of fair CRPS vs log10(N) for N>=50, and report the slope magnitude resolved in >=80% of resamples. Roughly $5-15 CPU; if even 92 HENS dates barely resolve the slope, the planned 7-date run is shown not worth pursuing before spending the $963.\",\"compute_after\":\"If underpowered, redirect the same dollars to many more dates at moderate N; only add members past ~100 on dates where the resampled slope CI excludes zero.\",\"exact\":\"Distribution over bootstrap resamples of the fair-CRPS-vs-log10(N) slope for N>=50 on 7-date subsets; report the effect size with >=80% detection rate and the date count needed for a modest slope.\",\"expected\":\"Seven dates resolve only a very large slope; roughly 30-50 dates are needed for a modest one, meaning the plan as written cannot answer its question at any member count.\",\"fails_if\":\"The bootstrap shows 7 dates already resolve small slopes with high power, in which case the original 1,000-member design is adequately powered.\",\"closest_prior\":\"HENS used 92 dates at up to 7,424 members [s_hens]; the plan inverts this to 7 dates at 1,000 members, and no prior result tests detectability as a function of date count.\"}]
